extracted.intended_audience: writers, students of rhetoric and literature, and critics seeking guidance on producing elevated/sublime style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on producing a noble, elevated (the Sublime) style in prose and rhetoric: what to avoid, how to handle vast scenes and detail, and the moral/intellectual habits that sustain great genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ignoble and vulgar expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: "'Wore away' is ignoble and vulgar, and 'unwelcome' inadequate to the extent of the disaster."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use low, commonplace or inelegant diction when treating lofty subjects; choose words worthy of the magnitude and seriousness of the event or theme, because mean phrasing reduces grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mix petty or mean details with grand subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixing up panniers and spices and bags with a wonderful recital of a vast and busy scene makes one imagine a kitchen; petty words introduced out of season stand out like deformities and blots on the diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid juxtaposing humble, domestic, or trivial items with magnificent elements in the same passage; such incongruous detail destroys sublimity. If less-important items must be mentioned, subordinate them or treat them collectively rather than spotlighting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give multitudinous details in broad strokes, not exhaustive enumeration
rubrics_metrics.description: These details might have been given in one or two broad strokes, as when he speaks of mounds being heaped together... or have mentioned 'piles of grain of every species, and of all the choicest delicacies required by the art of the cook or the taste of the epicure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing mass, plenty, or a vast scene, summarize with a few powerful, sweeping phrases rather than listing many petty particulars; broad, vivid generalities preserve grandeur and avoid cluttering the passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never stoop to what is sordid or despicable unless very hard pressed
rubrics_metrics.description: "In our sublimer efforts we should never stoop to what is sordid and despicable, unless very hard pressed by some urgent necessity. If we would write becomingly, our utterance should be worthy of our theme."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude gross, base, bodily, or offensive material from elevated passages unless a strong, necessary rhetorical reason demands it; follow nature's lesson of concealing grosser parts (citing Xenophon) to avoid marring beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inopportune petty words create conspicuous incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Petty words, introduced out of season, stand out like deformities and blots on the diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sensitive to the seasonal/tonal appropriateness of vocabulary; an oddly humble or trivial term in a lofty passage will attract notice and spoil the effect—revise to remove such blots or reposition them where they do not clash with the tenor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for nobility and loftiness; avoid elements contrary to the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: We have now pointed out the various means of giving [style] nobility and loftiness. It is clear, then, that whatever is contrary to these will generally degrade and deform it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the catalogue of positive means (grand diction, appropriate figures, concentrated energy, elevated thought) as a test: anything that conflicts with those principles will typically lower the style and should be removed or reworked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for lasting worth, not for pleasure, applause, or flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: If we ever apply ourselves to work, it is always with a view to pleasure or applause, not for that solid advantage which is worthy to be striven for and held in honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain intellectual and moral integrity: avoid composing from motives of servility, bribery, flattery, or the pursuit of transient applause. True genius and enduring works arise from striving for lasting value rather than pandering to tastes or gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pedantic, minute verbalism; rise to dignity and provide practical utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Caecilius is censured (1) as failing to rise to the dignity of his subject; (2) as missing the cardinal points; and (3) as failing in practical utility. He wastes his energy in tedious attempts to define the Sublime, but does not tell us how it is to be attained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute hair-splitting definition, petty verbal criticism, or excessive technicality for elevated insight and practical advice about how to achieve sublimity; aim for broad, useful principles and an expansive, elevated view rather than cold, minute scholarship that cannot guide practice.
